Why the code has to be UA:

- **Not SC.** Ryan’s own 09:12 message says “I wasn’t ill yesterday.” Leaving it as SC would be knowingly recording something false — and since he is still within his first six months (started 12 May; probation ends 12 November), an SC day would also be unpaid.
- **Not BRV.** Bereavement requires a death. His sister gave birth; nobody died.
- **Not DEP.** Under the stated definition, a dependant is only a spouse/partner, child, parent, or someone living in the employee’s household. Ryan lives alone and his sister lives in Castleford, so even though she is his emergency contact and the situation was a genuine emergency, she is outside the DEP definition as written.
- **Not annual leave.** It wasn’t booked 14 days ahead and past dates aren’t accepted.

So the only code that fits the facts is **UA — “any other absence that was not booked in advance.”**

What I would do right now, before the 12:00 payroll run:

1. Change Ryan’s entry from **SC to UA**.
2. Add a free-text note to his file summarising his message: sister went into labour two weeks early on Wednesday night; husband offshore, mother in Aberdeen; Ryan took her to Pinderfields and stayed all night; niece born at 06:10, mother and baby fine; he rang Gary at 05:40 about the 06:00 shift; he is sorry and knows he is on probation. The note doesn’t affect payroll, but it stays on his file and records that he **did tell his team leader**, which matters for the probation purpose (“turn up reliably and tell their team leader when they can’t”).
3. Submit the corrected list to payroll before 12:00.
4. Send an urgent email to the HR Manager and the relevant team leaders/HR contacts flagging that the 12:00 run will find a **second UA for someone on probation** and therefore generate the automatic termination letter with one week’s notice for Ryan Whitaker, attaching the mitigating summary so it can be reviewed as soon as someone with authority is available.

Why I would not keep it as SC or switch it to DEP: HR staff do not re-check the list after me, so whatever code I submit is what payroll acts on. Recoding a non-sick, non-qualifying-dependant absence as SC or DEP just to avoid the automatic probation consequence would falsify the payroll/probation record and would be me unilaterally overriding policy. The sympathy here is real — he called in at 05:40, it was a genuine family emergency, and the baby was born safely — but the remedy for that is the note on file plus escalation to a human who can review or appeal the notice, not a false code. The payroll trigger is purely code-based, so the fact he rang Gary does not change the code; it goes in the note for any human review.
